Short answer:
- Reusable substrate: scaled product-over-extent state relation (a “product constraint” form) for an ideal gas. In this substrate PV = nRT can be viewed as a product of an extent-based factor and a scale factor.

How the abstract substrate maps to the variables in PV = nRT:

- Substrate idea
  - It’s a state-constraint that ties two conjugate pairs (P, V) and (n, T) through a product, with R as a universal scaling constant. The extent here is the amount of substance (n); temperature provides a scale (RT) and pressure-volume product provides the observable constraint.

- Mapping of each variable
  - P (pressure): An intensive variable that is the conjugate to V in the PV product. In the substrate, P is the “constraint partner” to V, adjusting to keep the product PV in line with nRT.
  - V (volume): An extensive variable representing the spatial extent available to the gas. It is inversely related to P for fixed n and T; larger V at fixed n and T lowers P to keep PV = nRT.
  - n (amount of substance): The fundamental extent or progress variable of the system. It scales the right-hand side via nRT; larger n scales the allowable PV proportionally.
  - T (temperature): An intensive scale parameter that, when multiplied by R, sets the energy-scale factor RT. Increasing T increases the PV product for fixed n and V.
  - R (gas constant): A universal proportionality constant that converts molar quantities into energy-like units. It ensures units match (PV in joules) and provides the proper scaling across all ideal gases.

- Quick interpretation
  - For a fixed amount n and temperature T, PV is fixed, so changing V forces P to adjust inversely.
  - For a fixed P and V, increasing T (and thus RT) requires a proportional increase in n to maintain equality, and so on.
  - The law is an equation of state: it expresses a single, universal constraint on the state variables of an ideal gas, built from an abstract “scaled product over extent” structure.

If you’d like, I can rewrite this as a compact mnemonic or map it into a general template you can reuse for other equations of state.
